newsitem.title: UK: Britain tardy on N.Irish peace progress - Adams.
newsitem.headline: Britain tardy on N.Irish peace progress - Adams.

text.p: Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams accused Britain on Wednesday of blocking progress towards restoration of an IRA truce that he said had been wrecked by London's "cavalier" attitude.

"I continue to work with others to create the conditions for real talks in a peaceful environment. But there has been no indication so far that the British are really interested," said Adams, head of the Irish Republican Army's political arm.

His comments, in an article for the New-York based Irish Voice newspaper, cast a shadow over hopes of an early end to IRA violence after a weekend of mixed signals about the momentum for peace in troubled Northern Ireland.

The region's police chief warned last Sunday that the IRA was likely to launch more headline-grabbing attacks on British targets after a double carbomb last month killed a soldier inside British army headquarters near Belfast.

Hopes of political progress rose when it emerged that moderate nationalist leader John Hume had been in contact with Adams and the British government in a bid to end a deadlock between republicans and London and restore the IRA truce.
London, backed by Dublin, says Sinn Fein will get a seat in peace talks only if the IRA calls a new truce which is demonstrably genuine, and not simply tactical.

Sinn Fein says Britain squandered an IRA truce first called in September 1994 by refusing it access to negotiations and laying down demands for a handover of guerrilla weapons in a covert attempt to defeat the underground fighters.
Adams's article, the text of which was issued by Sinn Fein in Belfast, said Britain's approach to the original IRA truce had "subverted confidence" in a subsequent peace process.
British Prime Minister John Major "must show that he will not treat a second IRA cessation and a restored peace process in the same cavalier fashion as he did the last one," Adams wrote.
He asserted that Unionist politicians representing the majority pro-British Protestants had set their face against Sinn Fein's involvement in talks because they were afraid of change.
Unionist leaders would not engage in meaningful negotiations until the British government does, Adams declared.
